cards.title: The tracker dirties its own tree, so every piece of evidence is born unanchored

note.text: FINDING, caught by SW-044's own hand-back within a minute of shipping it. done() computes `dirty` from `git status --porcelain` over the whole tree. But .shipward/tracker.json is version-controlled here BY DESIGN — git is the authority, so the board is committed — and the MCP server rewrites mcp.lastSeen into it every 60 seconds as a heartbeat. The tracker file is therefore ALWAYS modified while a session is open. Measured at 10:46 on 2026-07-31: SW-044's check passed at 4ecfeaf with exactly one dirty path, `.shipward/tracker.json`, and nothing else. The consequence is not cosmetic: dirty:true makes freshness() report `unanchored` at birth, permanently, so no evidence this product ever writes can be current and the whole of SW-044 renders one state forever. SW-043's dirty caveat is equally defeated — it fires on every card and therefore says nothing. FIX, small: the tree that matters is the code under test, not the board describing it. Exclude .shipward/ when computing `dirty` in headState() — `git status --porcelain -- ':(exclude).shipward/'` or filter the porcelain lines — and say in the comment WHY the exclusion is honest rather than convenient: a tracker write is not a change to the thing the check exercised. Consider also whether the heartbeat belongs in tracker.json at all; mcp.mjs already records that tradeoff as chosen deliberately (one file occasionally dirty beat two files that can disagree), and this is the first real cost of it. Do NOT fix by dropping the dirty flag: a pass over genuinely uncommitted source is exactly the claim it exists to qualify.

cards.title: tracker-store.mjs is a binary file to git

note.text:
FOUND WHILE starting SW-039 on 2026-07-31: `git diff` on shipward/tracker-store.mjs prints "Binary files … differ" and shows nothing. git blame, code review and conflict resolution all degrade to nothing on it — and that file's own header comment enumerates eight separate lost-write bugs, so it is the last file in this repo whose changes should be unreviewable.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is NOT corruption: feedKey (line 79) was changed from .join(' ') to join on a NUL — a good hardening, since NUL cannot occur inside a timestamp, project id, author or message, so two entries can no longer collide by containing the separator. But it was written as a RAW NUL BYTE in the source rather than the escape. git's binary heuristic looks for a NUL in the first 8000 bytes; this one is at offset 4573, so the whole file is classified binary.

FIX is one character and semantically identical at runtime: write '\u0000' (or '\0') in the string literal instead of embedding the byte. The joined key is unchanged, so nothing about feed archiving changes.

Note for whoever picks this up: `grep` on this machine returns nothing at all (it is broken — verified 2026-07-31, it produced no output even for `grep -c ""`), so a NUL hunt with grep will report a clean file. Use node, or rg. That is also why this went unnoticed.

SHIPPED and pushed to main (c0d17b3). feedKey's NUL separator is now the escape form instead of an embedded byte — byte-identical at runtime, so no archived feed line changes. git classifies the file as text again, which is the whole point: shipward/tracker-store.mjs is the file whose header comment enumerates eight lost-write bugs, and its diffs were showing "Binary files differ".

FOUND WHILE starting SW-039 (which rewrites this file, so I needed its diffs readable).

GOTCHA worth keeping: git's binary heuristic only scans the first 8000 bytes, so this is silent for a NUL further in — and `grep` on this machine is broken (returns nothing for any pattern, verified with `grep -c ""`), so the usual NUL hunt reports a clean file. Use node or rg.
Check "default" (node --test) passed at c0d17b3, in 15082ms. That is what it proves: this command exited zero on this tree, not that the work is correct.

cards.title: Ignore .claude/worktrees — a stray add would commit a whole worktree

note.text: BRIEF. EnterWorktree and `git worktree add` both put worktrees under .claude/worktrees/, and .gitignore does not mention it — so `git status` on main shows an untracked directory containing a full second checkout, and one inattentive `git add -A` would commit it into the repo. Two are live right now (SW-043 and the concurrent session's bound-memory-reads). The fix is one line. Noted because the near-miss is not theoretical: this repo tracks 1,525 files under .claude/skills, so .claude is a directory people DO add wholesale.

SHIPPED to main. One line — `.claude/worktrees/` — plus the reason above it, because an ignore rule with no comment is the kind of line someone deletes while tidying. Committed straight to main rather than on a branch: switching branches in the shared checkout would have disturbed the concurrent session working out of it, and the change is one ignore line with no code path. Verified by the gate SW-043 added, which is the point of running it on something this small: the check ran against main's working tree while tracker.json was dirty with this very card's log entry, so the evidence records dirty:true and says it is not reproducible from the sha alone. That is the honest reading and it is what the caveat exists for.

Check "default" (node --test) passed at 07f4e7b with uncommitted changes in the tree, so this is not reproducible from the sha alone, in 16572ms. That is what it proves: this command exited zero on this tree, not that the work is correct.

cards.title: A check inherits SHIPWARD_TRACKER — a suite could reach the live board

note.text: FINDING, found while shipping SW-043. spawnCheck() does not set `env`, so the check inherits the server's environment — including SHIPWARD_TRACKER and SHIPWARD_REPO. A project whose check is its own test suite therefore runs that suite with a pointer to the LIVE board in the environment. This is the exact shape of the SW-033 incident, where a test sandbox resolved the real tracker through the cwd-first ladder and its PUT tests replaced 32 cards and 111 feed entries. It is not exploitable here today — the suite is proven byte-neutral against the real tracker, and that was re-verified by md5 before SW-043's own done() was allowed to run it — but the belt is a property of the suite, not of the runner, and the next repo to declare `checks: {default: [...]}` inherits no such proof. Options, cheapest first: scrub SHIPWARD_* from the child env (a check that genuinely needs them can be given them explicitly); or pass SHIPWARD_TRACKER pointing at a scratch copy; or leave it and say so in the docs. Decide before onboarding tells other repos to declare checks.

cards.title: Publish — licence, README, and strip the scaffolding before the repo goes public

note.text: BRIEF. Decision taken 2026-07-31: open source this under MIT rather than trying to charge for it. Reasoning, so nobody reopens it cheaply — there is nothing to gate (local-first, zero-dep, no auth, readable ES modules; a licence check is a three-line delete), the competition is free AND bundled with the tool you already pay for (Claude Code shipped built-in Tasks in v2.1.16), and distribution in this niche is stars, HN and the Claude Code ecosystem, where closed source is not premium, it is invisible. The asset is the judgment (git-as-truth tiers, note epistemics), which only pays out if it can be read. Timing matters: publish while 'Tasks has no repo awareness, no web UI, no MCP server, no git integration' is still true — Beads went from side project to absorbed-by-the-platform in months. WORK, all verified against the repo on 2026-07-31: (1) there is NO LICENSE and NO README at all; (2) git tracks 1,525 files under .claude/skills plus 72 under _bmad, none of which carry a bundled LICENSE file — third-party scaffolding that must be stripped or its terms verified before publishing; (3) a 43KB 'App progress tracker prototypes.zip' is committed at the root; (4) the shippable product is 26 files in shipward/, 3 in .shipward/, and CLAUDE.md; (5) design_handoff_shipward/ came from Claude Design — check what may be redistributed; (6) .shipward/tracker.json is real working memory about ten of Alberto's projects, including the incident write-ups. Publishing it is the single best demo this project has — a live board with real notes beats any screenshot — but read it end to end first, because it is a publishing decision, not a code one. README should carry the measurement that answers Beads' token argument: tools/list is 6,843 bytes (~1.7k tokens) for all six tools, measured 2026-07-31.

cards.title: A CLI surface so the protocol is not Claude-Code-shaped only

note.text: BRIEF. The four hooks are Claude Code specific, but the protocol is not — and today an agent that is not Claude Code has no cheap way in. Ship a thin CLI (shipward standup | log | start | done) over the same tracker-store and lib.js rules, so any agent that can run a shell command gets the protocol and any repo gets it without hook support. Cost is low: standup.mjs and status.mjs already run standalone by design. Secondary benefit — it strengthens an argument this project can already win. Beads' MCP README recommends CLI+hooks over MCP for Claude Code on token grounds, '~1-2k tokens vs 10-50k for MCP schemas'; measured 2026-07-31, this server's tools/list response is 6,843 bytes (~1.7k tokens) for all six tools, i.e. an MCP surface already at parity with their CLI. Worth stating in the README with the measurement, and worth a regression test so it stays true.

cards.title: Render through pure functions so the desk is testable without a DOM

note.text: BRIEF. SW-038 shipped a regression that no test could have caught: the fleet page's origin validator rejected the new ?fleet= URLs and silently unlinked every board — ten rows, zero anchors, no error — and it surfaced only in the live browser. That card already recorded the known limit (zero-dep means no jsdom, so row rendering has no DOM-level test). Fix it in the grain of the codebase rather than by adding Playwright and losing the zero-dependency story: push markup generation into pure functions in lib.js that take data and return strings, and test those under node --test — the same move that made fleetLinkFrom() testable. The bug class to target is producer/consumer drift, which is precisely what a pure function pins.

cards.title: The fleet answers questions — one standup across every board

note.text: BRIEF. fleet.mjs lists boards and spawns a desk per board; it does not yet answer anything that needs more than one board at a time. Add the aggregate view: one standup across every onboarded repo, what has been sitting in review longest anywhere, which repo has not shipped in N weeks, everything currently in flight. Mostly aggregation over the walk and the per-repo trackers that already exist. Strategic reason to prioritise it: cross-repo unification is the axis Alberto's 2026-07-10 sweep found agent-native tools worst at, AND it is the axis Claude Code's built-in Tasks structurally cannot reach — that system has no repo awareness and its task-list ids can collide across repos. Per-repo trackers (never pooled) plus a fleet that reads across them is the right shape and is already half-built.

cards.title: Trust panel — surface the reported tier the desk never shows

note.text: BRIEF. The reported tier is defined in git.mjs and deliberately never written by anything automatic — which means the most interesting data in the system is currently invisible. Give it a desk surface: cards claiming pushed whose commit is nowhere on the trunk, branches no card claims, files changed with no card in flight, review cards ageing past N days, notes carrying no evidence entry at all. Nothing here writes to the board — it reports, and a human decides, which is exactly the tier's existing rule. Why it matters commercially: the actual pain of running an agent solo is not knowing what happened while you were away, and every competing tracker assumes the agent's report is true. This repo has the machinery to contradict it and does not yet show the contradiction to anyone.

cards.title: Evidence expires — recall and the desk mark notes git has moved past

note.text: BRIEF. standup.mjs already says evidence rots — the PERISHABLE caveat, 'as of then, not a claim about now'. Make it mechanical instead of textual: an evidence entry carries the sha it was written against, and git.mjs can answer whether that sha is still reachable from HEAD and whether the files the entry concerned have been touched since. Then recall({file}) stops reporting '252 tests pass' flatly and reports '252 tests passed at 1942e8c — N commits have touched this file since', and the desk fades a verified badge as the work drifts out from under it. Pairs with the verification-gating card, which is what starts stamping shas onto evidence in the first place; this card is cheap once that exists. Positioning value: 'memory that knows it is out of date' is a claim no competitor in this category makes, and it is the natural headline for the write-up.

SHIPPED. Evidence entries now carry the sha they were true of, and standup/recall/the desk all read one freshness() verdict over a driftSince() map that asks git once per DISTINCT sha. FOUR STATES, and the design point is that the two ways of NOT knowing are kept apart: a sha git cannot resolve is `unknown`, never `fresh`, because a rebased-away or foreign sha answering '0 commits since' would render as still-current — a confident lie, which is the exact failure this card exists to remove. DECIDED: evidence with no sha keeps the old PERISHABLE wording rather than getting a second phrase for the same fact; a caveat that changes when nothing has changed teaches a reader to ignore it. A dirty tree IS new information, so that one speaks for itself. THE BUG WORTH REMEMBERING, and it cost the most time here: inside the SessionStart hook I declared `let drift` for the drift map, but `drift` is ALREADY the name of the git-audit function called three lines earlier in the same scope — so that call hit the temporal dead zone and threw, and the hook's own catch-all (Rule 1: never break a session) turned the crash into SILENCE. SessionStart emitted nothing at all: no standup, no audit, no error, exit 0. Six hook tests went blank rather than red, which is what caught it. A shadowed binding plus a fail-open catch is an invisible outage; the variable is named driftMap and the reason is written above it. SCOPE NOTE: /api/drift polls on its own 60s timer, not the tracker's 3s — the answer changes when commits land, a few times a day, and spawning git twenty times a minute for it would be absurd. VERIFIED IN THE BROWSER, which is the part no test covers (see SW-047): the Memory tab rendered 35 badges on 35 evidence entries and zero on any other kind, all reading 'unanchored' at 0.55 opacity — correct, because every entry on the board predates sha stamping. This card's own hand-back writes the first anchored one. 330 tests pass, up from 302.

Check "default" (node --test) passed at 4ecfeaf with uncommitted changes in the tree, so this is not reproducible from the sha alone, in 18237ms. That is what it proves: this command exited zero on this tree, not that the work is correct.

cards.title: Verification gating — done() runs the card's check and records what it proved

note.text: BRIEF. Strategy card, from a 2026-07-31 market read: Anthropic shipped built-in Tasks in Claude Code v2.1.16 (persistent via CLAUDE_CODE_TASK_LIST_ID, credited to Beads) and Beads now has a community web dashboard. The 'what should I work on next' half of this category is commoditised. The half nobody owns is 'prove it was done'. Today done() accepts a claim: the note nudge asks for prose, nothing checks the work. Build: a card carries a `verify` command (e.g. `node --test`); done() runs it, captures exit code plus the head of the output, and writes an evidence entry stamped WITH THE SHA IT RAN AGAINST. Three outcomes mirroring the git tiers in git.mjs — verified (ran, passed, at this sha), unverified (no check declared, and it says so rather than implying success), refuted (ran, failed: done is refused or the card returns to claude with the failure in the note). This is the existing thesis extended one step: git outranks the claim about the commit, the test run outranks the claim about the work. Alberto's 2026-07-10 sweep of 69 agents found verification gating 'barely exists anywhere'; it still does not exist as of 2026-07-31. It is also the hardest thing here to copy, because it only means anything on top of the tier and provenance machinery already in git.mjs and reconcile.mjs. DECIDED NOT TO BUILD (same session): dependency DAG, ready-queries, leases, multi-agent coordination — that is Beads' engine and competing on it head-on with a zero-dep solo project loses.

SHIPPED, and this hand-back is its own first demonstration: the check that gated it is the one it added. Built as designed in _bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/spec-verification-gating.md (ratified by Alberto before a line was written): checks are argv arrays declared by a HUMAN on the project, a card carries only a name, done() resolves and runs it, and the outcome is stamped with the sha and the cleanliness of the tree it ran on. TWO THINGS THE CODE CHANGED ABOUT THE SKETCH. (1) The check cannot run inside mutate(): mutate holds the cross-process advisory lock for the length of its callback and waiters give up at LOCK_TIMEOUT_MS=60000, so a suite inside one would not deadlock — it would starve the desk and every other session for as long as it takes. It runs unlocked between a read and a brief write, and a test pins the ordering by racing a standup against a 1.5s check. (2) A free-text verify command on a card is disqualifying: this file is written by an agent and by an unauthenticated PUT /api/tracker, so a command stored in it is an exec for anything that can write the tracker. Hence argv arrays, shell:false, and a card that can only SELECT. DECISION MADE DURING THE BUILD, not in the design: one rule for everything that was promised and did not pass — failed, timed out, could not spawn, OR named a check nobody declares. The first draft held the card on a timeout but promoted it on a typo, which would have made the gate optional by misspelling; that is the SW-038 failure mode (a feature silently doing nothing) wearing different clothes. WHAT A PASS CLAIMS, deliberately narrow: a declared command exited zero on a named tree. Not that the work is correct — the note says so in those words, because an agent that writes a passing test for broken code defeats this entirely. A pass over a dirty tree says that too, since it is not reproducible from the sha. 293 tests pass, up from 252: 33 new in verify.test.mjs (including the one that proves shell metacharacters are not interpreted and no file is created) and 8 in mcp.test.mjs. verification.sha is what SW-044 reads to expire this evidence; ok/at are what SW-045 counts. LEFT OPEN: the check inherits SHIPWARD_TRACKER from the server's environment — logged as its own card rather than buried here.
Check "default" (node --test) passed at d859d43, in 14800ms. That is what it proves: this command exited zero on this tree, not that the work is correct.

cards.title: standup’s "shipped in the last 7 days" list is uncapped

note.text:
FOUND WHILE filing SW-039..041 on 2026-07-31, by reading standup’s own output: every other list in standupText has a cap and an "…and N more" line — review 5 (standup.mjs:55), backlog 3 (:60), open STANDUP_OPEN (:82), decisions STANDUP_DECISIONS (:88). The shipped-in-7-days loop at standup.mjs:70 has neither, and on this board it printed 38 lines — 2,700 of the standup’s 4,574 chars, i.e. the majority of what a session is handed unasked.

Not a runaway: the window is 7 days, so it is bounded by throughput, not by time, and a quiet week costs nothing. But it is the one section whose size a burst week decides, and it is the least decision-relevant thing in the report — a session needs to know what it must not reverse and what is unresolved far more than it needs 38 titles of finished work.

Fix is the same shape as its four neighbours: a cap plus the "…and N more" line the others already carry. Deliberately P3 — this is a tidy-up, not a cost the way SW-039/040/041 are.

cards.title: recall caps entry count but not bytes

note.text:
MEASURED 2026-07-31 against this repo’s own memory (117 entries): mcp.mjs:330 renders each hit with line(e) and no max, so the COUNT is clamped to 50 (mcp.mjs:312) while the BYTES are not. recall({kind:"finding", limit:50}) returns 37,013 chars ≈ 9.3k tokens in a single tool result; kind:"outcome" 10,623 chars; kind:"decision" 7,754. The default limit of 10 keeps the common case near 2k, so this bites exactly when a session raises the limit — i.e. when it is hunting for something and least wants its context eaten.

standup already has the answer: line(e, {max}) and excerpt() are shared code this caller simply does not use. Fix is a max that tightens as the hit count rises, plus keeping the "raise limit to see them" hint honest by reporting that entries were CLIPPED as well as dropped.

SHIPPED on chore/bound-memory-reads (a116bf2). recall clamped how MANY entries came back (50) but never how long they were, because line() was called with no max while standup passed 240/200. Entries now share ONE budget (RECALL_BUDGET 9000 chars in standup.mjs) and each takes a share of it, floored at 320 and ceilinged at 1600 — a flat per-entry clip would be too mean for one hit and too generous for fifty. The floor deliberately wins over the budget: fifty entries clipped to 180 chars each is fifty entries that say nothing, and a caller only reaches fifty by explicitly asking.

FOUND WHILE FIXING IT, and fixed in the same card: the "files:" line was unbounded too — refs() pulls every path an entry names, and a note surveying a subsystem names dozens, so a text-only budget would have leaked straight through it. fileList() bounds it to 200 chars keeping WHOLE names, because a path clipped mid-segment is not a shorter path, it is a wrong one.

Clipped and dropped are reported as the different losses they are: one is an entry you never saw, the other an entry you saw the point of. Reporting only "…N more" while silently truncating the rest would make the answer read as complete.

MEASURED, old server vs new against this repo's own tracker (120 entries), same document: recall(finding,50) 37,685 → 9,740 chars (9.4k → 2.4k tokens); recall(outcome,50) 10,985 → 7,311; recall(decision,50) 8,544 → 6,283; recall(file:"shipward/mcp.mjs",6) 8,777 → 6,859.

TEST NOTE for whoever reads mcp.test.mjs next: "a reply larger than the pipe buffer is not truncated when stdin closes" (the SW-005 flush bug) built its >64KiB frame out of recall({kind:'finding',limit:50}). This card made that impossible, so the test was silently no longer testing the flush — it now builds the frame from standup's working-card titles, which are unclipped and uncapped. The assertion did not change; the vehicle did. If SW-042 ever caps that list, this test needs a new vehicle again.

261 tests pass, 9 new (4 in memory.test.mjs for noteDigest, 5 in mcp.test.mjs over the real pipe).

cards.title: start() hands back the whole note, unclipped

note.text:
MEASURED 2026-07-31: mcp.mjs:398 renders the handoff with noteText(card.note) and no clip, unlike standup, which passes a max to excerpt() (standup.mjs:82 uses 240, :88 uses 200). Biggest notes today — CA-011 6,187 chars ≈ 1.5k tokens, CA-013 5,511, SW-024 4,873 — and a card that is started repeatedly grows without bound. start() sits on the mandatory protocol path (CLAUDE.md rule 2), so every task pays this.

The machinery already exists: excerpt(entry, max) in public/memory-lib.js:191 leads with the point via pointIndex() instead of the preamble. The judgement call is that start() is the one surface where a session legitimately wants the WHOLE note — it is about to work that card. So the likely shape is: keep the most recent N entries in full, clip the older ones, and SAY how many were clipped and that recall reaches them. A silent truncation here would be worse than the tokens, for the same reason recall reports its dropped count.

SHIPPED on chore/bound-memory-reads (a116bf2). start() now renders the note through noteDigest() instead of noteText(): the newest 3 entries exactly as before — that is the state a session is resuming and it should arrive whole — and everything older clipped to 400 chars through the same excerpt() standup already used, which leads with the point rather than the preamble. The reply says how many entries were clipped.

DECISION worth not reversing: the pointer for the full note is the desk and .shipward/tracker.json, NOT recall. recall clips too (SW-041), so "call recall for the rest" would have been a promise this server cannot keep.

MEASURED, old server vs new against the same live documents: CA-011 6,187 → 4,265 chars (1,547 → 1,066 tokens, 4 entries clipped), CA-013 5,672 → 4,741, CA-012 4,513 → 3,754, SW-024 4,873 → 3,286.

KNOWN LIMIT, stated rather than hidden: a card whose newest 3 entries are themselves huge is still unbounded — SW-019, SW-015 and SW-020 have 3 or fewer entries and so clip to nothing, still handing back ~4,200 chars (~1k tokens). That is the design the card specified and it is defensible (you want the state you are resuming), but if start ever needs a hard ceiling, this is where it is missing. Also: noteText() now has no production caller — it survives as a public function of memory-lib with its own test, not as dead code, but nothing would break if the desk never picks it up.

cards.title: Archive shipped cards’ notes out of the hot tracker

note.text:
MEASURED 2026-07-31 on this repo’s own board: .shipward/tracker.json is 138 KB across 38 cards (15 pushed, 23 shipped), and note text is 69% of those bytes (95 KB). Catch’s tracker: 47 KB / 13 cards, notes 73%. Cards are never deleted by protocol and notes are append-only, so the hot file only grows — nothing does for card notes what FEED_CAP + feed-archive.jsonl (tracker-store.mjs:65, :106) already do for the feed.

The cost is NOT the standup: that is capped by design (STANDUP_OPEN/STANDUP_DECISIONS, entries clipped to 240/200) and measures ~4.4k chars ≈ 1.1k tokens on this tracker, roughly flat as the board grows. The cost is the MCP-offline fallback CLAUDE.md documents as supported — "read → modify → write the whole file" — which is ~35k tokens to read and a full rewrite to save, scaling linearly with the file. It also makes git diff on the tracker unreadable, and the tracker is committed to git precisely so it can be recovered by hand (see the SW-033 clobber).

The design question to settle BEFORE code: where do shipped-card notes go, and how does recall still reach them? feed-archive.jsonl can be write-only because nothing ever reads it back; card notes cannot, because recall({file}) is the mandatory pre-edit step (CLAUDE.md rule 0) and a finding filed under a long-shipped card is exactly what it must still surface. So the archive needs a reader, or the split has to be by entry age/kind rather than by card status.

cards.title: A way back — the desk links to the fleet that opened it

note.text: Alberto, on the desk: where is browser back? A desk opened from the fleet had no way home but browser chrome — invisible in the Claude Code pane. Fix: the fleet appends ?fleet=<its origin> to each desk link; the desk renders a home link in the header when, and only when, that param names a localhost origin. Validated by a pure lib function, because a URL taken from the query string and rendered as a link is exactly how open-redirect decorations get in.

SHIPPED. fleet.mjs stamps each desk link with ?fleet=<origin>; app.js reads it once through lib_s fleetLinkFrom(), which accepts ONLY http://localhost:port or http://127.0.0.1:port — javascript: urls, real domains, localhost.evil.com and path-carrying values all die in the test suite, because a link rendered from a query parameter is an open redirect wearing a home icon. A desk opened without the param (bookmark, manual serve) shows no link at all.

REGRESSION, CAUGHT LIVE, MY OWN BELT: the fleet page_s SW-034 defence — a strict origin-only regex before rendering desk hrefs — rejected the new ?fleet= URLs and silently UNLINKED every board (10 rows, zero anchors, no error anywhere). Producer grew, consumer_s pattern did not. Fixed by parsing with new URL() and checking what actually matters (http, local host, bare path), which survives the next parameter too; the producer_s URL shape is now pinned by an assertion in fleet.test. LESSON: a validator written as a snapshot of today_s shape is a regression waiting for the first evolution — validate properties, not spellings. KNOWN LIMIT: the fleet page_s row rendering still has no DOM-level test (zero-dep, no jsdom), which is exactly why this only surfaced in the live browser.

VERIFIED as the full round trip in the live pane against the launchd service (kickstarted twice to pick up code): fleet → click Shipward → desk header shows ← fleet linking to http://localhost:4740/ → click → back on the fleet. 252 tests pass (fleetLinkFrom acceptance/rejection table, producer URL shape).

cards.title: The fleet starts itself — a launchd agent, installed by script

note.text: Alberto: start the fleet automatically so I do not have to run it. macOS answer: a user LaunchAgent — RunAtLoad + KeepAlive, logs to ~/Library/Logs/shipward-fleet.log. Shipped as shipward/fleet-service.mjs install|uninstall|status rather than hand-written machine config, so it is redoable on any machine and the plist generation is testable as a pure function. Node is pinned by absolute path (process.execPath at install time) because launchd has no shell PATH.

SHIPPED. fleet-service.mjs install [root] | status | uninstall. Needs the explicit apply.   reported — git can only raise a question: not-on-trunk, no-branch, untracked-branch. Never written. SAFETY PROPERTY WORTH KEEPING: the reconciler is MONOTONIC. Every certain rule only ever confirms progress git can prove — in-flight to pushed, blank to sha. Nothing walks a card backwards, so a human who moves a card ahead of git is never overruled by it. cards.title: sync reads git itself — derive status instead of asserting it

note.text: The (b) angle from the divergence exercise, narrowest useful slice. sync today applies fixes but requires Claude to work out the truth from git and hand it over, so it only corrects drift someone already noticed. DESIGN: shipward/git.mjs does the I/O and nothing else; the rules live in a pure deriveFindings(cards, facts) so they are testable without a repo, the same split lib.js uses. Six rules, each from a real slip: a commit that is not an ancestor of main on a pushed card; a missing commit where the branch has one; a merged branch on a card still in claude or review; a branch with commits against a backlog card (my SW-005 slip); a claude card with no branch at all; and a feat/fix/chore branch no card references. Structure mirrors lib.js — readGit does I/O and nothing else, deriveFindings is pure — so the rules are tested exhaustively with hand-built facts and readGit is tested once against a real throwaway repo, because a mock of git would only prove I can predict git, which is the thing in doubt. Explicit updates beat derived ones — git is the better witness but the caller may know something git cannot see. THE BEST THING THAT HAPPENED: the tool's FIRST real run produced a false positive about the very card being written on it. Rule 3 used `git branch --merged`, and a branch cut from the trunk tip has no commits of its own so git lists it as merged — 'no work yet' and 'work landed' are indistinguishable by that signal. Rewrote it to key off a recorded commit proven to be an ancestor of the trunk, which is unambiguous AND keeps working after the branch is deleted, the normal state after a merge. A tool that audits drift finding its own bug on first contact is the strongest argument for it that I could have asked for. cards.title: MCP cancellation is accepted and ignored

note.text: Deferred from SW-020, deliberately. notifications/cancelled is accepted and then ignored: the cancelled call keeps running, still writes, and still holds the write queue behind it. Real cancellation means carrying an AbortSignal from the notification through callTool into mutate() and the cross-process file lock, and deciding what a half-applied mutation means — a lock holder cannot simply be abandoned. That is a larger change than the finding warrants, and bodging it would be worse than the honest gap. The blast radius today is small: a client that cancels gets no reply and the write lands anyway.

IMPLEMENTED, and the deferral reasoning in the brief above turned out to be answerable rather than blocking. THE SHAPE: cancellation is best-effort with a DEFINED COMMIT POINT, which is the only honest version of it. A queued call never runs. A running one is abandoned inside mutate() just before the write, lock released and file untouched. While waiting for the lock, acquire() checks the signal on each retry, so a cancelled call stops occupying the write queue instead of blocking whatever is behind it — that was the part I had assumed needed a big change and did not. Past the rename the write is durable, so the work finishes; cancelling there would mean inventing an undo. Either way NO response is sent, per the protocol. DESIGN CALL: CancelledError is its own type, not a tool failure — nothing went wrong and nothing was written, so it must not surface as an errored result the model would read and retry. An unknown or already-finished requestId is ignored, because a reply and a cancellation crossing is the normal race. TESTING GOTCHA WORTH KEEPING: my first cancellation test PASSED against the pre-fix server, which nearly let a non-test through. It was racing the write it was meant to catch — it used tools/list as its barrier, and SW-020 had just made protocol frames stop waiting on the write queue, so the barrier no longer barred anything. Serialising behind a tools/call fixed it, and both tests then failed against the old code as they should. A test that passes before the fix is not a test. 173 tests pass, 4 new.

cards.title: MCP server: the Blind Hunter's 13 findings

note.text: THREE SERIOUS. (1) DATA-LOSS: no tool argument is ever checked against its own inputSchema, and validate() in tracker-store checks every card field EXCEPT note — while schema.json declares note as a string. So log({note:42}) is accepted, written verbatim, and then permanently bricks the entire memory surface: standup and recall both throw, the session-start hook emits ZERO BYTES so the session silently gets no standup, and status.mjs drops its count. Cards cannot be deleted by protocol, so recovery needs a hand-edit. (2) SESSION-BREAKING: the startup heartbeat is queued AHEAD of the handshake, so initialize cannot answer until a tracker WRITE completes — measured 5.8s behind a held lock and 62s when the lock is never released. A handshake bounded by LOCK_TIMEOUT is a server the client declares dead. (3) SESSION-BREAKING: process.exit(0) on stdin end discards unflushed stdout, so any reply over the 64KiB pipe buffer is truncated mid-JSON with exit code 0 — measured, last frame exactly 65525 bytes and unparseable. recall({query:'e',limit:50}) is already 32775 bytes against the real tracker, half the cliff. THE REST: a non-numeric limit prints a total then lists nothing; sync(create) bypasses the empty-title guard log enforces and writes permanent junk cards; the 1000th card of a prefix makes log fail forever with an opaque schema error; requests with no id (or id:null) get invalid frames back and a tools/call notification still WRITES; done({pushed:true}) on an already-pushed card claims a stamp it never wrote, so it never counts as shipped; sync files its single feed entry under the default project even when every card it touched is in another; the provenance stamp carries no year so a three-year-old note looks like yesterday; the idempotent start path still tells Claude to create a branch that already exists; and we advertise protocol revisions in which batching is legal, then refuse batches.

FIXED, 12 of 13. THE DATA-LOSS ROOT CAUSE was one missing line: validate() checked every card field EXCEPT note, the one field the whole memory surface reads and one schema.json already required to be a string. Tool arguments were never checked against their own inputSchema either, so both halves were open. THE HANDSHAKE FIX is architectural rather than a patch: there are two chains now, because tools/call takes the lock and must queue, while initialize/ping/tools/list must never wait on the tracker at all — a handshake bounded by LOCK_TIMEOUT is a server the client declares dead. Output drains before exit, the same defect and the same fix as the hooks in SW-018. Batches are now HANDLED rather than refused, because we negotiate revisions in which they are legal and refusing them was advertising a version we did not implement. NOT FIXED, deliberately: notifications/cancelled is still accepted and ignored, so a cancelled call keeps running and still writes. Real cancellation needs the tool layer to carry an abort signal through mutate() and the file lock, which is a bigger change than the finding warrants today — filed rather than bodged. TESTING NOTE WORTH KEEPING: I could not verify these tests against the pre-fix code the way I did for SW-017/18/19, because the pre-fix suite HANGS rather than fails — 8m20s with no result. That is itself the confirmation for the hang-class findings, but it means the other nine rest on the reviewer's reproductions plus the fixed-state tests, not on a watched red-to-green transition. 169 tests pass, 9 new.
Merged to main. Cancellation is NOT fixed and is tracked as SW-021.

cards.title: Tracker lock: the layer under the SW-010 fix

note.text: Edge Case Hunter over tracker-store.mjs. FIRST, THE FIX HOLDS: 1600/1600 writes landed with 0 lost, and 2083/2100 on a harder run where ~4 losses were expected at the old rate. The one-observation inspect() and link-a-complete-scratch publish() genuinely closed SW-010. TEN FINDINGS UNDER IT. F1 lost-write, SILENT: held() is checked before atomicWrite, but the commit is open+write+fsync+chmod+rename — measured p50 5.17ms and max 16.17ms on a realistic 43KB tracker, the same order as LOCK_RETRY_MS, not microseconds. A card vanished with no error raised anywhere. F2 corruption: breakLock renames the lock to a grave BEFORE checking the inode, so a third process can publish into the freed path and the link-back then unlinks that innocent holder lock; F2 is F1 trigger. F3 permanent deadlock: alive(pid) makes a lock unbreakable FOREVER — a lock 24h old held by pid 1 timed out at 60s and never becomes breakable. The lock lives in the repo working directory so it survives a reboot, after which the pid is very likely someone else. F4 permanent deadlock: release() swallows unlink errors, so one transient EACCES leaks a lock carrying a LIVE pid and wedges that daemon for its whole lifetime. F5 permanent deadlock: age<0 means NEW with no upper bound, so an mtime one hour in the future is immortal and any backwards clock step immortalizes every existing lock. F6: the heartbeat utimes a PATH, so a dispossessed holder keeps a corpse fresh forever and a third writer fails at 60s. F7: a provably dead holder still costs 30s, and LOCK_TIMEOUT is only 2x LOCK_STALE, so two crashes inside one waiter deadline is a guaranteed failure — 2 of 4 clean writers hard-failed. F8: no fairness, 17 of 2100 writes timed out and ALL 17 were the same starved process. F9: withLock is not re-entrant, a nested mutate is a silent 60s hang. F10: graves are never swept, neither sweep regex matches .lock.dead.<uuid>. NEGATIVE RESULTS WORTH KEEPING: 4000 create/delete cycles produced 4000 distinct inodes on APFS so the F2 guard is sound here, but ext4/HFS+ recycle aggressively and it would false-negative there; publish() partial writes are not reproducible; link() on FAT/network mounts is untested and would fail with a raw errno and no diagnosis.

FIXED, 9 of 10. THE PRINCIPLE THAT CHANGED: liveness is a hint, the heartbeat is the evidence. A living holder refreshes its mtime every second, so silence past LOCK_ABANDONED_MS (5 min) is abandonment whatever the pid says — that single reframing closed F3 (a live pid made a lock unbreakable FOREVER, and the lock survives a reboot after which the pid is someone else's) without reopening SW-010's slow-but-alive bug. F1, the silent lost write: held() now runs at the last instant before rename rather than before a 5-16ms commit, so nothing is published by a holder that no longer holds. F5: a future mtime is bounded at 5s — beyond that it is a broken clock, not sub-millisecond precision, and unbounded it made locks immortal. F7: a provably dead holder costs 2s not 30, because the pid check already proved it gone; at the old grace two crashes inside one waiter deadline was a guaranteed failure. F4: release retries and then warns loudly instead of swallowing. F2: breakLock re-reads and aborts if the lock is no longer the inode it condemned. F6: the heartbeat verifies the token before touching, so a dispossessed holder can no longer keep a corpse fresh. F9: a nested mutate throws immediately. F10: graves are swept on age. F8 partially — jittered backoff spreads the cost but is still not a queue; a true FIFO would need a ticket file and that is a bigger change than the starvation warrants. NEGATIVE RESULT WORTH KEEPING: the inode guard is sound on APFS (4000 create/delete cycles, 4000 distinct inodes) but ext4 and HFS+ recycle aggressively and it would false-negative there; link() on FAT or a network mount is untested and would fail with a raw errno and no diagnosis. 160 tests pass, 5 new. Contention stress re-run clean at 2700 writes with 0 lost.
Merged to main. F8 (fairness) is only partly addressed — jittered backoff spreads the starvation but is still not a queue. Named here rather than left implied.

cards.title: Status line and hooks: terminal injection, truncation, and a hang

note.text: The Blind Hunter BROKE the invariant I claimed for the status line, on its first try. FINDING 1, worst of the day: status.mjs interpolates card text straight into stdout with nothing stripped, so tracker data becomes terminal control. Proven with real output — a title containing \u001b]0;PWNED\u0007 rewrites the terminal/tab title, \u001b[2J\u001b[H clears the screen, \u001b[?1049h switches to the alternate screen buffer, a bare \r overwrites the line just drawn, and a newline turns a one-line status line into three. TITLE_BUDGET is no mitigation: the clear-screen payload is 7 characters. Worse, the card ID is never clipped at all and status.mjs never calls validate(), so ID_RE does not apply to it. U+202E RTL override passes through too. CLAUDE.md blesses hand-editing and log() takes free text, so this is data the tool invites. FINDING 2: emit() in the hooks writes then calls process.exit(0), which drops whatever has not flushed — a hard cliff at exactly 65536 bytes on a pipe. One card with a 70KiB title makes every hook emit unparseable truncated JSON, and past ~1000 cards the write is lost entirely so the STOP HOOK SILENTLY STOPS BLOCKING. It fails open, which is the wrong direction. FINDING 3: the stdin read has no timeout, so a pipe held open hangs the hook until the runtime kills it — on UserPromptSubmit that is a stall every single turn; 600MiB of stdin was also buffered in full. FINDING 4: the PreToolUse matcher includes NotebookEdit but the handler reads tool_input.file_path, and NotebookEdit passes notebook_path, so it can never warn. Also: clip() splits emoji into lone surrogates; openItems() does an uncapped memory scan on every render (390ms at 1000 cards); and activeLine() injects card text into the model context every turn with no framing that it is data.

FIXED. Every value that reaches the terminal is scrubbed of C0, DEL, C1, the bidi overrides and the line separators, and the card ID is now bounded like the title — it was neither clipped nor validated, since status.mjs never calls validate(). Hook output is bounded BEFORE the write and drained before exit: over the bound it says less correctly instead of more corruptly, and the Stop hook can no longer fall silent, which was how it failed OPEN. GOTCHA WORTH KEEPING: my first stdin-timeout fix used AbortSignal.timeout and did nothing — a for-await blocked on the next chunk never reaches a condition it could check; the stream has to be DESTROYED on a deadline. The regression test caught that, which is the only reason I know. SECOND GOTCHA, on the nose: the tool refused to run my own command for containing raw control characters while I was writing the tests for control characters — the payloads are now built from String.fromCharCode so no literal control byte exists in the repo. Also fixed: NotebookEdit was in the PreToolUse matcher but the handler only read tool_input.file_path while NotebookEdit passes notebook_path, so it could never warn; the open-item scan is skipped past 400 cards (390ms at 1000, 1.6s at 5000) rather than stalling the render; clips no longer split an emoji into a lone surrogate; and activeLine now labels card text as tracker data, because a card can be logged from an issue body and its title reached the model context unframed on every turn. 155 tests pass; 8 new, each verified to fail against the pre-fix code.

cards.title: Harden memory-lib against the edge-case review

note.text: Edge Case Hunter returned 15 CONFIRMED findings against public/memory-lib.js, every one reproduced with a script. THREE ARE SERIOUS. (1) resolves() matches RESOLUTION markers by substring with no polarity check, so 'Not yet fixed — parked until he answers' marks an open item SUPERSEDED: the card says the question is open and the module reports zero open, dropping it from stillOpen, standup, recall and the status line. The module's stated purpose, inverted. (2) A non-string note throws — validate() in tracker-store.mjs never checks `note`, and CLAUDE.md explicitly calls hand-editing supported, so note:12345 passes readRaw and then kills standup, the memory view and both MCP tools; status.mjs swallows it and prints '◇ no card', which is a lie. cards.title: Ambient status line — know without looking

note.text: The ambient angle from the 2026-07-27 divergence exercise. THE OBSERVATION THAT MADE IT WORTH BUILDING: the UserPromptSubmit hook is already an ambient surface and is the highest-frequency Shipward surface that exists — it fires on every single prompt, while the board gets opened a few times a day. You do not want to LOOK AT the board, you want to know without looking. A Claude Code statusLine is the terminal-native version of that: always visible, nothing to open, no window to arrange. SCOPE: shipward/status.mjs prints one line — the active card, what is waiting on the human, and how many memory items are still open — wired into .claude/settings.json as statusLine, and runnable standalone so it also works in a tmux or shell prompt. CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES THE WHOLE THING: it is re-rendered constantly, so it must be FAST and must never break a terminal. That rules out importing tracker-store.mjs (crypto, full schema validation) — a plain readFileSync and JSON.parse is the whole data path — and it means every error prints nothing and exits 0.

SHIPPED. shipward/status.mjs prints one line — card in flight, what is waiting, how many memory items are still open — wired as statusLine in .claude/settings.json and runnable standalone for a shell prompt or tmux. MEASURED, because 'fast' was the whole constraint: 121ms per render, of which 107ms is bare Node startup; the script itself costs 14ms and 10 of those are the memory pass. That is why it does NOT import tracker-store.mjs — hashing, full schema validation and crypto are pointless for a read-only glance; readFileSync plus JSON.parse is the entire data path. MEASUREMENT GOTCHA: a shell for-loop first reported 1.1s per render, which sent me looking for a blocking call that did not exist. Timing ten spawns from inside node gave 121ms. Do not trust a shell loop for sub-second benchmarks. DESIGN CALLS: the mark carries the state without colour (filled diamond in flight, hollow idle) so a terminal that drops colour still reads; counts render only when non-zero, because a line that always says '0 review · 0 backlog' is furniture and furniture stops being read; only the title is ever clipped, never the id or the counts; NO_COLOR is honoured. HARMLESS RULE, tested by spawning: a missing tracker, an unparseable tracker and a document with no projects each print NOTHING and exit 0 — a status line that throws leaves a broken terminal and no explanation. 133 tests pass, 10 new. WHY THIS ANGLE: the UserPromptSubmit hook was already an ambient surface and the highest-frequency one in the product; this is the same idea given a permanent place. NOT YET SEEN IN THE RUNTIME — like the hooks, it needs a session rooted at shipward_app to render for real.

cards.title: Hooks — make the Shipward protocol continuous, not aspirational

note.text: WHY, with evidence from this very session: CLAUDE.md, the MCP instructions field and the tool descriptions are three layers of ADVICE and nothing checks. Proof they are not enough — I built the entire MCP server for SW-005 without ever calling start; the card sat in Backlog while 500 lines were written against it, and I only noticed by running standup for an unrelated reason. If the author of the protocol, holding it in active context, drifts inside one session, advice is not a mechanism. FOUR HOOKS: SessionStart injects a standup so a session begins already knowing; UserPromptSubmit injects one line naming the active card EVERY TURN, which is the actual continuous part because drift cannot accumulate; PreToolUse on Edit/Write warns when source is about to change with no card in claude/working — WARNS, never blocks, because a hook that gets disabled protects nothing; Stop refuses to end while a card is still working with no done. DESIGN RULES: a hook must never be able to break a session, so every one exits 0 silently on any error; the Stop hook honours stop_hook_active so it cannot loop; and the standup text is extracted into a shared module so the hook and the MCP tool cannot drift apart. KNOWN LIMIT stated up front: hooks can make Claude TOUCH Shipward, they cannot make it write a good note — done with 'fixed it' satisfies every one of them and teaches the next session nothing.

SHIPPED. .claude/settings.json wires four hooks to .claude/hooks/shipward.mjs: SessionStart injects a standup unasked; UserPromptSubmit injects one line naming the active card EVERY turn (the continuous part — drift cannot accumulate); PreToolUse on Edit/Write/NotebookEdit warns when source changes with no card in claude/working; Stop refuses to end while a card is still working with no done. TWO RULES THE HOOK FILE MUST NEVER BREAK, both covered by tests: (1) a hook can never break a session — every path exits 0 and any failure (missing tracker, unparseable tracker, unknown subcommand) exits silently, because a broken hook that bricks the project is worse than no hook; (2) pre-edit WARNS and never denies — permissionDecision is always 'allow' — because a hook that gets in the way gets switched off and a switched-off hook protects nothing. Stop honours stop_hook_active or it would refuse the session forever. pre-edit exempts .shipward/, .claude/, _bmad-output/, .git/ and CLAUDE.md/README.md: touching those proves nothing about the protocol, so nagging is pure noise. REFACTOR THAT CAME WITH IT: standupText/line/stamp/PERISHABLE moved out of mcp.mjs into shipward/standup.mjs so the SessionStart hook and the MCP tool render from ONE implementation — two renderings of the same board would tell a session two different stories. 123 tests pass, 11 new, spawning the real script the way the runtime does (payload on stdin, JSON on stdout). MEASURED COST: ~90ms per prompt hook, dominated by node startup rather than reading the tracker; paid on every turn. NOT YET VERIFIED IN THE RUNTIME — the hooks are unit-tested against the documented wire shapes but have never actually fired inside Claude Code. That needs a session rooted at shipward_app plus hook approval. KNOWN LIMIT, stated up front: hooks can make Claude TOUCH Shipward, they cannot make it write a good note; done with 'fixed it' satisfies all four and teaches the next session nothing.

NOT YET PROVEN IN THE RUNTIME even though it is now on main: the hooks are unit-tested against the documented wire shapes but have never fired inside Claude Code. First session rooted at shipward_app will need to approve them.

cards.title: Close the memory loop — standup carries it, recall retrieves it

note.text: THE GAP, measured: the tracker holds 27 memory entries / 4044 words, and standup returns 0 of them. The only path back is start, one card at a time, so Claude retrieves memory about the ticket it is opening and never about the code it is about to touch. From the agent's side this store is write-only. FIX: (1) standup gains a bounded memory section — decisions not to reverse, and still-open items, each with its card id and date; (2) a new recall tool takes file / kind / query and returns the entries attached, ranked by what it would cost to miss. DESIGN RULES: every entry arrives with its date and card so a session can judge rather than believe; evidence is labelled as a claim about a PAST state, because 'tests pass' rots (45 was true this morning, it is 96 now); nothing is silently truncated — recall says what it dropped and how to get it. Standup stays readable: entries are clipped with the card id kept so the full text is one recall away.

SHIPPED. standup now carries a bounded memory section (still-open items + decisions not to reverse, each stamped with card and date, clipped so the full text is one recall away) and a new recall({file|kind|query}) tool retrieves the rest, ranked by what it would cost to miss, always reporting what it dropped. TWO THINGS THAT ONLY SHOWED UP ON REAL DATA: (1) BRIDGING FILE TO PROSE — SW-010's note, the most valuable in this repo, names NO file at all; it names isStale(), breakLock(), sweepTmp(), because that is how you write down what went wrong. recall({file}) therefore reads the file off disk and asks about every name declared inside it, not just the filename. Before the bridge, recall({file:'tracker-store'}) returned one irrelevant hit; after, six with both SW-010 findings ranked first. (2) DROPPING GENERIC NAMES — tracker-store.mjs declares 73 names and most are now()/read()/line(), so matching any of them returned the whole tracker and the top hits were unrelated. Tokens appearing across more than a quarter of the memory are now dropped before scoring, and entries rank by how many distinct names they match. GOTCHA IN THAT FIX: the share filter then ate EVERY token on a small corpus, because with two entries one hit is already 50 percent — recall returned nothing at all. Nothing counts as generic until it has turned up at least 4 times; regression test covers the young-repo case. cards.title: A live lock is broken as stale — silent lost write

note.text: REPRODUCED while fixing SW-009. The 12-writer store test fails about 1 run in 6 under full-suite load: 11 of 12 cards land, every child exits 0, nothing is logged. A high-cycle harness (6 processes x 150 mutations) loses ~1 write per 900 reliably. ROOT CAUSE: isStale() judges the lock from TWO separate observations of the path — readHolder() then lstat() — and the lock can be replaced between them. When readHolder() hits the lock in its momentary absence (normal, between one holder release and the next publish) it returns null, and lstat() then measures a DIFFERENT, brand-new lock. That new lock trips `if (age < 0) return true` — the line commented "clock skew: as broken as too old". Measured: st.mtimeMs carries sub-millisecond precision while Date.now() truncates to whole ms, so a freshly created lock reads as up to 0.62ms in the FUTURE in 1085 of 2000 observations. Over half of all new locks are therefore condemned the instant that race is hit. Trace confirms the full chain: break-won by a waiter, then 6ms later the true holder gets release-skip (its lock is gone) and its atomic-write chmod fails ENOENT because breakLock -> sweepTmp deleted the live holder’s in-flight .tmp. Two writers in the critical section, one write silently overwritten. THREE DEFECTS: (1) isStale reads stat and content from different observations; (2) age < 0 is treated as death when it actually means brand new; (3) sweepTmp unlinks temp and lock-scratch files belonging to LIVE processes.

FIXED. inspect() now reads mtime, inode and holder from ONE open handle, so a stat and a read can never land on two different locks. A future mtime means new, not dead (the old 'age < 0 = as broken as too old' line was the trigger). breakLock() compares the grave's inode against the snapshot it judged and puts an innocent lock back. sweepTmp() only collects files whose pid is dead. withLock() hands callers a held() guard checked immediately before the commit, so a lost lock raises LockLostError instead of overwriting whoever holds it now. EVIDENCE: before, ~1 write lost per 900 under sustained contention (2 of 4 trials) and the 12-writer test failed ~1 run in 6 under full-suite load; after, 12960 contended writes across 14 trials with zero lost and six consecutive clean suite runs. 49 tests pass. Three new regression tests were each run against the PREVIOUS store and all three fail there: future-dated lock read as a corpse, sweep eating a live process's in-flight temp, and a mid-write lock loss writing anyway.

cards.title: Cross-process safe tracker writes — shared store + lock

note.text: Stage A of SW-005. Extracted read/validate/atomic-write into shipward/tracker-store.mjs behind an O_EXCL advisory lock spanning the whole read-modify-write; serve.mjs is now a client and its in-process promise chain is gone. That chain only protected same-process writes — the MCP server and Claude Code direct edits both sit outside it. Lock records pid+timestamp, aged out after 5s so a crashed holder cannot deadlock the desk. 34 tests pass: store.test.mjs spawns real child processes (12 concurrent writers all land, stale locks broken, fresh locks waited for not stolen, invalid mutations write nothing and still release); desk-core suite passes unchanged as the regression gate. ⚠️ PULLED BACK FROM REVIEW 2026-07-25: adversarial review REPRODUCED five failures — the lock does not hold. (1) Contended stale-break: 4 processes vs one stale lock, 9/25 trials LOST WRITES, because detect-and-break is three non-atomic steps and each breaker unlinks the previous winner’s fresh lock. (2) A 6s mutation gets its lock stolen at 5s; both processes exit 0 and one write vanishes silently. (3) A dangling symlink at the lock path spins acquire() forever at 100% CPU — two of three loop paths skip the deadline check. (4) replace() (every card drag) never re-reads under the lock, so a desk PUT erased a Claude write that had committed correctly. (5) rename resets file mode 600→644. Also: feed at exactly 200 makes validate() reject every subsequent write and freezes the tracker; lost in-process FIFO ordering; GET re-serializes instead of returning raw bytes. 34 tests passed throughout — none of them covered contention.

REWORKED after review: the lock was redesigned, not patched. Publish via write-scratch-then-link(): link is atomic AND never leaves an empty lock visible, which open(wx) did — under contention a process starved between create and stamp, waiters read a bodyless lock and broke a LIVE holder’s. Break a dead lock by rename (one atomic step) so two breakers cannot both win and delete each other’s fresh lock. Ownership token: a holder only ever releases the lock it took. Liveness (process.kill(pid,0)) over age, plus a utimes heartbeat — utimes not writeFile, because rewriting the body truncates it and reopens the same window. Every retry path now checks the deadline and sleeps (two used to spin at 100% CPU). Also: feed cap truncates instead of rejecting (rejection froze the tracker permanently at 200 entries); file mode preserved across rename; fsync before rename; read() distinguishes ENOENT from EACCES; GET returns raw bytes not a re-serialization; in-process FIFO queue restored in front of the lock; err.name instead of instanceof; orphan tmp and lock-scratch files swept on break. 41 tests pass. Stress: 25 trials x 4 contended writers against a stale lock = 0 lost writes, 0 leftovers (was 9/25 losing writes). 12-writer repro 12/12 across three runs.

cards.title: PUT /api/tracker is last-write-wins — decide if it should be

note.text: REPRODUCED by adversarial review against a live server: desk GETs at T0, Claude Code appends a card via mutate() at T1 (correctly locked, committed), desk PUTs its T0 snapshot at T2 — PUT 200 and Claude’s card is GONE. The lock worked perfectly and the data was still destroyed, because replace() never re-reads under the lock: its base document came from an unlocked GET seconds earlier. This is the primary remaining loss path. It is also a CONTRADICTION between two live contracts. spec-mcp-tracker-server.md Always says two processes must never start a mutation from the same base document; spec-shipward-desk-core.md accepts no optimistic concurrency on PUT, last write wins, as a documented assumption. NEEDS ALBERTO: either add optimistic concurrency (If-Match on a version or etag, 409 on conflict, UI re-reads and retries) which is an Ask First change to the HTTP surface, or narrow the stage-A Always to say the lock protects mutate() callers only and PUT stays last-write-wins by design. Referenced from a comment in tracker-store.mjs replace().

DECIDED by Alberto: add optimistic concurrency. GET returns an ETag (content hash); PUT requires If-Match and answers 409 with the current document when it does not match; the UI re-applies its mutation to the fresh document and retries once. This is the authorised Ask First change to the HTTP surface. [committed by Claude at T1]

SHIPPED: GET returns an ETag (sha256 of the file bytes, 16 hex chars, quoted). PUT requires If-Match — 428 without it — and the store compares it INSIDE the lock against what is on disk. Mismatch answers 409 carrying the document that actually won plus its ETag, so the client can re-apply rather than guess. The UI recovers automatically: commit() takes a mutation, not a snapshot, so on 409 it re-applies the same intent to the winning document and retries once; a second conflict adopts the winner and says so. VERIFIED end to end against the live server by replaying the exact scenario the review used to destroy data: desk GETs at T0, Claude commits via mutate() at T1, desk PUTs its T0 snapshot at T2 — now HTTP 409 and Claude’s write SURVIVES. In the browser: drag sends a well-formed If-Match; a forced stale etag produced 409 then 200 with the external write intact and no error shown. 45 tests pass. The old "concurrent writes never corrupt the file" test was rewritten — it asserted six concurrent PUTs from one base all succeed, which was the bug; it now asserts exactly one wins and the rest get 409.
